content: Crohn's disease in children is a chronic condition characterized by periods of relapse and remission. Between 15% and 40% of children with this disease experience growth retardation. While certain treatments, such as corticosteroids, have been associated with growth failure, the primary cause is believed to be the uncontrolled activity of the disease itself. Growth is a critical aspect of pediatric care, and addressing growth failure is of paramount importance to patients, their families, and pediatricians. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of various treatment strategies for childhood Crohn's disease in reversing growth failure and promoting normal growth. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including EMBASE, MEDLINE, The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and others. Abstracts from major gastrointestinal research meetings and references from published articles were also reviewed. The review focused on randomized controlled trials involving children under 18 years of age with Crohn's disease, specifically those that included growth as an outcome measure. Data extraction and evaluation of the methodological quality of each trial were independently performed by two reviewers. However, only one high-quality randomized controlled trial was identified, which precluded the possibility of conducting a statistical analysis. Three randomized controlled trials were ultimately identified. One high-quality study (Markowitz 2000) investigated the use of 6-mercaptopurine (6-MP) as a steroid-sparing agent. This study found no significant difference in linear growth between the 6-MP group and the placebo group. However, the total steroid dose administered over an 18-month follow-up period was reduced in the 6-MP group. The other two trials (Sanderson 1987; Thomas 1993a) compared enteral feeding with corticosteroids for inducing remission, using height velocity standard deviation scores at six months as an outcome measure. Although these studies were of lower methodological quality, their findings were discussed in detail. Both studies demonstrated that height velocity standard deviation scores were significantly higher in the enteral feeding group compared to the corticosteroid group. In addition to these randomized controlled trials, lower-quality evidence exists regarding other interventions. These include the use of supplemental enteral nutrition and surgical interventions in pre-pubertal children with refractory disease. Studies such as those by Morin (1980), Belli (1988), and Israel (1995) have explored supplemental enteral nutrition, while surgical interventions have been examined in studies by Alperstein (1985), Lipson (1990), and McLain (1990). Emerging treatments, such as infliximab, are increasingly being used and may offer potential benefits in promoting growth, although their effects on growth have not yet been studied. This review underscores the urgent need for large, multicenter studies to evaluate the various treatment options for pediatric Crohn's disease. It also highlights the importance of using standardized growth measurements, such as height velocity standard deviation scores and height standard deviation scores, as key outcome measures.
